entry.title: Exploring AI and key innovations in SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS2
entry.content:
SAP is building the Autonomous Enterprise — an operating model where AI is not a separate tool but a force embedded directly into the operational core, executing work end to end. The SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS2 (also referred to as SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS2) release accelerates this shift, expanding agentic AI across finance, supply chain, asset management, sales, service, and product design.

At the top sits Joule — the new engagement layer where people, data, workflows, and agents come together across SAP systems and beyond. Underneath, the SAP Autonomous Suite reimagines how enterprises run through three coordinated layers:

  • Joule Assistants are role-aligned AI teammates — each designed around a specific business function such as financial closing, cash management, or logistics. They understand your context and coordinate the right agents to deliver the outcome you need.
  • Joule Agents are the specialized doers. Each agent handles a specific multi-step task — calculating accruals, screening maintenance requests, resolving invoice discrepancies — reasoning over live business data and acting autonomously within defined guardrails.
  • Embedded AI features power everyday Fiori applications with natural-language search, smart summarization, AI-assisted filtering, and error explanation — intelligence built directly into the screen, no agent orchestration required.

Industry AI adds vertical depth — process knowledge, compliance rules, and data models specific to your industry, embedded from day one. And the SAP Business AI Platform provides the foundation everything runs on: unified data, business context, and enterprise-grade governance.

 

*Disclaimer: The Joule Assistants and Agents described in this post are currently available through SAP's Early Adopter Care (EAC) program. General availability is planned to begin in Q4 2026, with rollout continuing into Q1 2027. Not all agents require SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS2 — minimum system requirements vary by agent, and support for additional releases is being continuously extended through downports. For the latest on which releases support which agents, refer to SAP Note 3789370, which is updated on an ongoing basis, and the SAP Discovery Center. All other AI innovations covered in this post (embedded AI features, Joule skills, and machine learning scenarios) are generally available with the 2025 FPS2 release unless noted otherwise. This blog is a living document and will be updated as new assistants and agents become available in the coming weeks and months. The information here reflects publicly available SAP product documentation and roadmap materials as of October 2026. All forward-looking statements are subject to change.

 

With this release, SAP significantly expands both the number of assistants and the depth of agent coverage across the suite. Here is what is new.

Part A: Joule Assistants and Agents

 

Finance: Autonomous Intelligence Across the Financial Lifecycle

Finance is the largest area of AI investment in FPS2, with new agents and assistants organized across the Autonomous Finance portfolio — from accounting and close, to treasury, revenue management, and compliance.

Financial Closing Assistant

 

The Financial Closing Assistant orchestrates the agents managing the period close, with users controlling each agent's level of engagement for handling journal postings, clearing activities, and analysis. Its tasks include: clearing receivables and payables; calculating and posting accounting accruals; posting journal entries; resolving errors and detecting anomalies in asset accounting; analyzing financial consistency and surfacing bottlenecks; reconciling goods receipt/invoice receipt and intercompany transactions (including matching unstructured intercompany invoices); managing fixed-asset master data and reviewing general ledger accounts; and clearing general ledger balances with final review, KPI analysis, and executive-summary generation. assistant is coordinated by the Financial Closing Orchestration Agent and includes the Journal Entry Agent for recommending and posting general-ledger entries with an evidence trail, the Accounting Accruals Agent for analyzing historical data and preparing accrual journal entries, the Receivables and Payables Clearing Agent, the Financial Consistency Analysis Agent for identifying hidden process inconsistencies and the Asset Accounting Anomaly Detection Agent for flagging potentially inaccurate postings. (SAP Discovery Center | Learn more).

 

 

Accounts Receivable Assistant

 

The Accounts Receivable Assistant helps finance teams accelerate cash collection, resolve disputes efficiently, and manage credit risk proactively, providing a 360-degree customer view that surfaces overdue items, balances, dispute cases, promises to pay, resubmissions, and contact history. Its capabilities span collection worklist management, dispute management, and dunning insights — focusing collectors on critical accounts, surfacing next-best-action recommendations, preparing customer communications, creating and resolving disputes from emails or Joule prompts, and analyzing payment history with AI-based matching and aging-pattern analysis. The assistant coordinates specialized agents: the Accounts Receivable Orchestration Agent, the Collection Account Preparation Agent for delivering instant account insights and preparing collection calls, the Dispute Creation Agent for creating dispute cases and validating documents and duplicates, the Dispute Resolution Agent for providing context and recommending resolution actions, the Dunning Insights Agent for analyzing payment history and providing AR recommendations and the Receivable Account Analysis Agent for visibility into balances, invoices, aging, disputes, and dunning levels.(SAP Discovery Center | ).

 

 

Accounts Payable Assistant

 

The Accounts Payable Assistant transforms AP with AI-powered automation — eliminating manual payments, automating bank validations, and resolving exceptions instantly while predicting payment risks, detecting clearing patterns, and surfacing real-time insights on DPO, aging, and cash flow. Its capabilities span six areas: payment inquiry, which captures requests, triggers payments, and sends status updates; pre-validation, which validates attributes, checks compliance, performs risk checks, and recommends fixes; bank validation, which verifies supplier bank accounts, automates risk checks, and recommends corrective actions; exceptions, which flags, explains, and routes payment exceptions; vendor analytics, which tracks DPO, cash flow, and discount opportunities and identifies operational improvements; and reconciliation, which reconciles statements and highlights discrepancies. The assistant coordinates with specialized agents: the Accounts Payable Orchestration Agent and the Receivables and Payables Clearing Agent for AI-based matching and aging-pattern analysis to generate clearing recommendations. (SAP Discovery Center | ).

 

Recurring Receivables Assistant

 

The Recurring Receivables Assistant helps finance teams automate and optimize the order-to-cash process for recurring billing and subscription-based business models, deploying finance agents that accelerate cash collection, resolve disputes, and identify and act on revenue at risk. Its capabilities span convergent invoicing, subscription contract changes, invoice correction orchestration, collections prioritization, dispute resolution, 360-degree customer account visibility, and payment matching with continuously improving matching rules. The assistant coordinates with specialized agents: the Subscription Lifecycle Agent for managing subscription contract changes with compliant updates, the Convergent Invoice Execution Agent for detecting invoice issues and executing compliant fixes and the Collection Insights Agent for recommending next-best actions prioritized by cash impact and customer insights.(SAP Discovery Center | ).

 

Sales: Agentic Order Fulfillment and Expanded Conversational Capabilities

Sales Operations Assistant

 

The Sales Operations Assistant enables sales teams to quickly identify fulfillment issues, receive recommended resolutions, and create or update sales documents directly in their workflow — minimizing manual rework and delays, reducing order-to-cash cycle time, and improving customer satisfaction. Its capabilities span two core areas: order entry, which supports uploading unstructured purchase-order files, extracting and validating data, reviewing order requests, and converting them into sales orders; and order monitoring and issue resolution, which covers supply, credit, billing, and delivery issues — including recommending corrective actions, removing blocks, and creating or updating sales documents after human approval. The assistant coordinates with specialized agents: the Billing Block Resolution Agent, the Credit Block Issues Resolution Agent, the Delivery Issue Resolution Agent, and the Supply Issue Resolution Agent (SAP Discovery Center | ).

 

 

Supply Chain, Manufacturing, and Logistics

The supply chain and manufacturing areas receive targeted AI enhancements in FPS2, with a focus on production planning intelligence, quality management automation, and warehouse operations support.

Logistics Assistant

 

The Logistics Assistant brings AI-driven coordination to warehouse operations, helping keep day-to-day logistics running efficiently. In this release for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, it focuses on two critical areas: batch lifecycle management and warehouse resource optimization. On the batch side, the assistant continuously monitors batch expiration across inventory and triggers actions to minimize waste — ensuring perishable or time-sensitive goods are consumed or moved before they expire. On the warehouse floor, it facilitates optimal resource allocation by analyzing workload patterns and proactively flagging potential resource shortages before they impact operations. The assistant coordinates with two specialized agents: the Batch Optimization Agent, which autonomously tracks expiry timelines and initiates corrective actions, and the Warehouse Workload Optimization Agent, which balances labor and capacity to keep throughput on target (SAP Discovery Center | Learn more).

 

 

Asset Management: A New Level of Intelligence for Maintenance and Operations

Asset management receives the most comprehensive agent expansion in this release, with a suite of new Joule Agents — orchestrated by the Asset Operations Assistant — designed to support the entire maintenance lifecycle from equipment onboarding to job debriefing.

 

Asset Operations Assistant

 

The Asset Operations Assistant orchestrates AI agents across reliability, maintenance planning, scheduling, and execution to turn asset signals into coordinated maintenance action and improve uptime. It interprets equipment signals and requests to prioritize work, aligns resources and readiness, and uses execution outcomes to continuously improve asset performance. Its tasks include: assessing asset alerts and recommending next-best actions; creating and prioritizing maintenance work based on asset conditions, business priorities, and operational needs; optimizing maintenance schedules and workforce assignments; and briefing technicians and summarizing completed work. The assistant coordinates six specialized agents: the Equipment Insights Agent for complete equipment insights supporting better decisions, planning, and reliability; the Maintenance Event Planning Agent for avoiding disruptions with real-time insights, smart updates, and planning support; the Maintenance Job Debrief Agent for streamlining maintenance job debriefs with AI-driven recommendations and insights; the Maintenance Request Initiation Agent for instantly creating and routing maintenance requests from natural language inputs; the Maintenance Task List Management Agent for automating task list creation, boosting consistency, and reducing effort; and the Operational Maintenance Planning Agent for avoiding disruptions with real-time insights, smart updates, and planning support (SAP Discovery Center | Learn more).

 

R&D / Engineering

 

Product Design Assistant

 

The Product Design Assistant is an AI-driven system of agents that connects data across product development and downstream processes. It analyzes product information, supports change decisions, ensures compliance, and coordinates collaboration — helping teams move faster, reduce rework, and deliver higher-quality products. Its tasks include: analyzing product designs, recipes, and specifications; preparing product changes including scoping and assessing impacts; validating compliance and requirements across product and recipe data; extracting, classifying, and improving product data quality; setting up collaborations, tracking tasks, and creating notifications; and preparing product data for handover to production and supply chain execution. The assistant coordinates two specialized agents: the Change Record Management Agent for reducing cost and accelerating time-to-market and the Product Data Maintenance Agent for assisting design engineers who work with product master data in SAP S/4HANA (SAP Discovery Center | Learn more).

 

Procurement

 

Receiving Assistant

The Receiving Assistant is a new Joule Assistant for procurement that simplifies goods receipt, service entry sheet processing, and returns by automating tasks, streamlining workflows, and guiding users through complex receiving scenarios. In this release, the assistant introduces the Return Goods to Supplier Agent — a specialized agent that detects goods with slow or no movement in inventory and optimizes and automates the returns process back to the supplier. Instead of requiring procurement or warehouse teams to manually identify stagnant stock, investigate root causes, and initiate return purchase orders, the agent continuously monitors inventory movement patterns and triggers the returns workflow autonomously. This reduces the manual effort involved in identifying returnable goods, accelerates the returns cycle, and helps organizations recover value from unused or slow-moving inventory. The result: lower carrying costs, improved working capital, and a cleaner inventory position — all driven by machine learning rather than periodic manual reviews (SAP | Learn more).

 

Part B: Embedded AI Innovations

 

AI-assisted enterprise search in the SAP Fiori launchpad to search for form bundles and contract objects

 

AI-assisted enterprise search in the SAP Fiori launchpad extends natural-language search to form bundles and contract objects, allowing users to type plain-language queries in the launchpad search bar and retrieve relevant results without navigating complex filter structures. The feature targets a larger and more specific result set from less-specific queries, reducing the time users spend locating the right form bundle or contract object. It builds on the broader AI-assisted enterprise search capability already available in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition for objects such as sales orders, billing documents, and purchase orders — and is listed as a future release for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (SAP Discovery Center).

 

AI-Assisted Enterprise Search for Service Contracts

This feature extends natural language search in the SAP Fiori launchpad to service contracts, enabling users to find contracts using plain language queries with instant responses. It eliminates the need to learn system syntax or complex filters, simplifying adoption and reducing training needs while delivering results in a single search interaction.

 

AI-Assisted Defect Creation (Quality Management)

Joule now enables quality engineers and technicians to create defect records through natural language — including from uploaded source documents such as invoices, delivery notes, or photographs of a defective part. Instead of manually navigating screens and populating fields, users simply describe the issue or attach a document, and Joule extracts the key data — material number, batch, quantity, reference documents, customer or supplier information, defect description, and defect code — then calls the Defects API to create a pre-filled record. The capability supports Generic Defects, Production Defects, and Warehouse Defects (types 06, 07, and 08). Once created, users review and complete the defect in the Manage Defects app. Under the hood, the feature runs on the QM_DEFECT_DOCSUMMARY intelligent scenario and requires activation through Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM). Available from 2025 FPS02 (SAP Help).

 

AI-Assisted Enterprise Search for Bill of Distribution (BOD) 

Enables natural language search for bill of distribution data, simplifying navigation and accelerating access to critical logistics information for planning and distribution teams.

 

AI-Assisted Enterprise Search for Batches in the SAP Fiori Launchpad

This feature extends natural language search to batches within the SAP Fiori launchpad, displaying key data including shelf-life expiration date, manufacturing date, batch status, country of origin, supplier, material, and plant. It enhances the search experience by allowing users to find batch data using everyday language.

 

AI-Generated Business Insights in Cost Center Review Booklet (Finance)

 AI-generated summaries now enhance the cost center review booklet, providing deeper financial oversight by analyzing and validating both actual and planned cost data. Business users get faster, more informed analysis with insights that would previously have required manual review of multiple reports.

 

 

Performance and Flexibility for Behavioral Insights (Collections Management for Contract Accounting)

SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition includes an AI-supported capability called Behavioral Insights for Contract Accounting — a machine learning solution that analyzes historical customer data to predict and explain payment risk. Collection specialists use these risk scores and insights to quickly identify high-risk accounts, optimize collection strategies, and reduce outstanding debts and write-offs. Results integrate directly into existing dunning and collections workflows.

The 2025 FPS2 release strengthens this capability across three dimensions. First, performance enhancements now support significantly larger datasets within the models, enabling organizations with high-volume receivables to run predictions at scale. Second, flexibility enhancements introduce support for multiple contract account categories within a single solution — a change that directly enables public sector organizations managing multiple tax types to leverage behavioral insights across their full portfolio. Third, a new ability to accommodate test datasets where the data may not be current makes it easier and faster to validate and deploy machine learning scenarios in non-production environments.

A key architectural advantage remains: the solution keeps data in place within SAP S/4HANA, eliminating the need for data extraction or replication. This reduces deployment risk, accelerates time to value, and ensures that sensitive customer data never leaves the system boundary.

 

 

Create Sales Orders from Unstructured Data with Document AI (Sales)

Internal sales representatives can now create sales orders directly from purchase order files in PDF, email, or image formats. The system leverages premium Document AI (AnyDox) to automatically extract file information and propose values for sales order fields — with multi-language support and instant learning capabilities. This significantly reduces manual data entry and accelerates order processing, especially in high-volume environments.

 

AI-Assisted Management of Expiring Service Contracts with Joule Skill (Service)

This feature enables users to search for expiring service contract items within a user-defined time frame via Joule and run extension scenarios including configuring auto-renewal, renewing and creating new service contracts, renewing entire contracts or specific line items, and providing quick actions for expiring contracts. It allows service teams to manage contract tasks through natural language requests, providing fast navigation and targeted guidance for renewing or extending contracts.

 

Joule-Based Search and Status Update of Service Contracts with Joule Skill (Service)

Users can now search for service contracts or contract items by employee and product name directly in Joule, and change lifecycle status to "released" or "complete" within the same conversational experience. This combines search and updates in a single interaction, reducing clicks and context switching while minimizing administrative overhead for contract managers.

 

 

AI-Assisted Processing of Incoming Quality Certificates

This capability, cross-ported from SAP Cloud ERP, automates the extraction and validation of data from supplier quality certificates. It delivers immediate efficiency gains by reducing manual effort in quality management — a high-usage area where even small improvements have a significant impact. In parallel, Joule for App Navigation in Quality Management now enables users to instantly navigate to more than 15 core QM Fiori apps using natural language queries.

 

Master Data Management

 

Joule for Data Provider Integration in Business Partner Governance

This feature enables users to search for business partner reference records from external data providers directly within Joule, display details including name, address, and identification numbers, and create a business partner from a selected reference record with pre-populated fields. It simplifies data governance through a conversational interface, improves data quality, and reduces manual entry by transferring reference data directly into the creation flow.

 

Joule for Business Partners — Central Governance

Users can now ask Joule in natural language to search, display, and edit business partner data, including address, communication, bank, and identification data. This delivers a consumer-grade experience for master data processing, increasing effectiveness, speed, and automation in business partner governance. Available in cloud-ready mode in SAP Master Data Governance.

 

 

AI-Assisted Validation Rule Creation in Joule

Joule can now create validation rules using AI, automatically deriving values such as the base table from a provided description. It also checks for duplicates to determine if a similar rule already exists in the system — increasing efficiency, reducing manual effort, and maintaining system integrity.

 

User-Experience

 

AI-Assisted Filtering Using Natural Language for SAP Fiori Elements Apps

Users can now filter list report applications built with SAP Fiori elements using conversational terms alongside system-defined filters. The feature supports query reuse, including saving favorite queries and accessing last-used ones — making data access more intuitive across all Fiori elements-based applications.

 

AI-Assisted Explanation of Errors in SAP Fiori Elements-Based Applications

This feature provides AI-generated explanations for error messages in SAP Fiori elements apps, offering solution proposals directly within the framework. It increases productivity by minimizing downtime from data entry errors and reduces training time through clear, natural-language guidance.

 

AI-Assisted Smart Summarization of Application Content

Users can generate AI-driven summaries for business object pages in SAP Fiori elements applications, then edit and copy them for sharing with stakeholders or external parties. It simplifies access to vital business data through one-click functionality and boosts productivity by supporting faster, informed decision-making.

 

Note: This blog focuses on the AI and Joule innovations that bring the most meaningful business impact in this release. It is not an exhaustive list of all enhancements — for the full scope of what's new, check out the resources linked at the end. A comprehensive release blog covering all innovations across every Line of Business is being prepared by Harish Mangtani and will be published in the coming days. Follow Harish on SAP Community to get notified when it goes live.

 

Looking Ahead

With the 2025 FPS2 release, SAP Cloud ERP Private (also referred to as SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition) continues to demonstrate that the future of enterprise work is not about adding AI on top — it is about building intelligence directly into the fabric of business processes. Every agent and assistant introduced in this release is designed to reduce manual effort, improve data quality, support faster decisions, and ultimately help your teams focus on the work that matters most.

The innovations in this release are part of SAP's broader vision for the Autonomous Enterprise — where Joule Assistants coordinate specialized Agents across all business functions, powered by SAP's deep process expertise and real-time business data. The pipeline of assistants and agents continues to expand rapidly. Additional assistants are expected to follow in the near term. This blog will be updated as new capabilities reach Early Adopter Care or general availability. For the latest status on all available agents, check the SAP Discovery Center and SAP Note 3789370.

If you want to explore the full scope of innovations in this release — including non-AI enhancements — I encourage you to check out the following resources:

entry.title: Building CAP Agents for Knowledge Work - Announcing Two Vector-Store CDS Plugins
entry.content:
A CAP Agent can continue a conversation and, with a long-term Memory Store which I made 2 weeks ago, can remember useful information across conversations. But a support agent also needs to answer questions from product guides, troubleshooting notes, or company policies.

That knowledge already exists in documents. The agent needs a way to find the relevant passages and use them when answering a question.

In this post, let's focus on that retrieval layer. I'm introducing two open-source vector store add-ons for CAP-level Agents:

  1. @mi8y/cap-agents-aicore-vectorstore (npm package link & source code), backed by SAP AI Core Document Grounding
  2. @mi8y/cap-agents-cds-vectorstore (npm package link & source code), backed by CDS entities in the application's database.

The concept itself is not new, RAG has already past the trend. But the use-cases surrounding it have evolved into Agentic RAG to enable building Knowledge Agents. The above two CDS plugins help build such agents with CAP-level Agents.

We'll use the same knowledge-agent pattern for both: ingest a text file, split it into chunks, retrieve relevant passages, and pass those passages with their source information to the agent.

Remembering information and finding information

Conversation state, long-term memory, and document retrieval serve different purposes:

Capability What it provides Example

CheckpointerConversation state, resumability, HITL, fault toleranceResume an interrupted interaction
Memory StoreRemember facts across conversationsRemember a user's communication preference
Vector storeKnowledge grounding from indexed contentFind the procedure described in a support guide

When a user asks a question, vector-store retrieval finds passages that are semantically relevant. The application then supplies those retrieved passages to the model as context. This is the retrieval part of Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG. For AI Agents which rely on knowledge-based task reasoning, vector-stores provide the necessary mechanisms to retrieve and ground relevant information, while working on tasks.

For example:

User: What does company policy say about data retention?
   [Tool]: Retrieves the relevant section of the company policy from ingested documents
Agent: Answers using that section and identifies the source.

Retrieval gives the model evidence to work with. Its usefulness still depends on the content, chunking, retrieval quality, and how the agent uses the results.

Two ways for CAP-level Agentic RAG

Both packages implement LangChain's VectorStore interface. That gives application code familiar methods such as addDocuments(), similaritySearch(), and asRetriever().

The main difference is where the knowledge base lives and who manages the lifecycle of embeddings and the retrieval.

  AI Core Document Grounding CDS vector store

ImplementationAICoreVectorStoreCDSVectorStore
Content and vector storageSAP AI Core Document Grounding collectionCDS entities in the CAP application's database
Embedding generationSAP AI Core Doc Grounding service generates and manage embeddingsConfigured LangChain embedding implementation
RetrievalGrounding Retrieval APICAP's Vector & cosine similarity operation
Initial setupExisting collection and AI Core connectionAutomatically created CDS entities along with embedding configuration
Useful fitA managed grounding serviceInfrastructure owned and operated within a CAP application

Note that, I have not added specific database requirements for the CDS vector store, because CAP handles database interactions and similarity search internally, abstracting away handling the vector operations.

If you are looking for managed grounding services, my recommendation is SAP AI Core Document Grounding. SAP provides collection, document, and retrieval APIs and helps abstract away a lot of generating and managing embeddings & text as well as complex retrieval operations.

The CDS approach is useful (I prefer for standalone agent implementations) if you'd like to keep the knowledge base closely tied to one application (say for quick PoCs or one-off requirements) and keeping it in that application's persistence makes development and operations simpler. It uses CAP's Vector type and database similarity search; See vector embeddings guide.

Both packages are open-source and MIT licensed. They provide retrieval adapters for CAP applications and can be used with @cap-js/agents.

Two Vector Stores for CAP Agents

Getting started with a knowledge agent

The following walkthrough uses CAP Node.js 10 or later, LangChain, and SAP AI Core credentials. Configure the agent's model and AI Core connection for your environment using the official CAP Agents documentation and SAP AI SDK connection guide.

See fully functional examples:

  1. Example 1: CAP Agents AI Core Vector Store Example
  2. Example 2: CAP Agents CDS Vector Store Example

Create an application if you do not already have one:

cds init my-knowledge-agent
cd my-knowledge-agent
cds add nodejs
npm install @cap-js/agents @SAP-ai-sdk/langchain \
  @langchain/core @langchain/textsplitters langchain zod

Choose one of the following vector-store configurations. In either case, save the configuration as srv/lib/vector-store.js. The ingestion handler and agent tool below import this file.

Option 1: SAP AI Core Document Grounding

Install the adapter:

npm install @mi8y/cap-agents-aicore-vectorstore

Create a Grounding collection separately and configure its embedding model. Follow SAP's Vector API and Pipelines API documentation.

Then connect the adapter to the collection:

import { AICoreVectorStore } from "@mi8y/cap-agents-aicore-vectorstore";

export const vectorStore = new AICoreVectorStore({
  collectionId: "<document-grounding-collection-id>",
  aiResourceGroup: "default",
  destination: { // optional if using a specific AI Core destination
    destinationName: "<aicore-destination-name>"
  }
});

The adapter needs no CDS model for vector persistence and no client-side embedding implementation. SAP AI Core Document Grounding as a managed service in BTP completely take care of storing the supplied chunks, generates embeddings according to the collection configuration, and performs retrieval.

This example (see repository here) prepares chunks in the CAP application and writes them through the Vector API.

Option 2: CDS persistence with SAP AI Core embeddings

Install the CDS adapter and generate its persistence entities:

npm install @mi8y/cap-agents-cds-vectorstore
cds add agent-cds-vectorstore

The command creates db/agent-cds-vectorstore.cds with Documents and DocumentMetadata entities. Deploy them as part of the regular CAP database lifecycle.

Configure the store with an embedding client:

import { CDSVectorStore } from "@mi8y/cap-agents-cds-vectorstore";
import { AzureOpenAiEmbeddingClient } from "@sap-ai-sdk/langchain";

const embeddings = new AzureOpenAiEmbeddingClient({
  modelName: "text-embedding-3-small",
});

export const vectorStore = new CDSVectorStore(embeddings, {
  name: "knowledge-base",
  threshold: 0,
});

Here the SAP AI SDK generates embeddings through SAP AI Core, while content, metadata, and vectors are stored in the CAP application's database.

By default, the CDS entity model uses Vector(1536) column for storing embeddings, matching the default output of text-embedding-3-small. But for higher-dimensional embeddings required for text-embedding-3-large models, you need to adjust the column dimensions accordingly i.e. Vector(3072). Point here is - keep the stored dimension and embedding model configuration consistent. If you change the model or its output dimensions, update the model and re-index existing content as needed. Document and query embeddings must use compatible configurations.

The name separates logical stores in the same tables. This helps to keep different collections logically distinct.

For production, use a supported database configuration such as SAP HANA Cloud or Postgres. For local development, CAP supports vector operations in SQLite too.

Prepare and ingest the documents

For AI Core Document Grounding-based Vector Store setup using the Pipeline API, the API handles the ingestion process, including chunking, embedding generation, and storage for a connected document source such as Microsoft Sharepoint, Object Storage, SAP Document Management service or other supported repositories. Hence, this is applicable only while using Vector API approach for Document Grounding service as well as CDS-based Vector Store.

Your application takes care of extracting/converting to plain text before splitting it into chunks for embedding. Then the vector store takes care of generating embeddings, storing and managing the embeddings.

import { Document } from "@langchain/core/documents";
import { RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter } from "@langchain/textsplitters";

// create a text splitter to divide large documents into smaller chunks
const splitter = new RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter({
  chunkSize: 1000, // adjust based on your requirement
  chunkOverlap: 200,
});
const chunks = await splitter.createDocuments([buffer.toString("utf-8")]);

// map individual text chunk into 'Document' type
const documents = chunks.map(
  (chunk, index) =>
    new Document({
      id: `${fileId}:${index}`,
      pageContent: chunk.pageContent,
      metadata: {
        sourceId: fileId,
        source: file.fileName,
        chunk: index,
      },
    }),
);

// finally embed and add the documents to the vector store
await vectorStore.addDocuments(documents);

Chunk size and overlap are starting values. Evaluate and adjust them based on whether a retrieved passage contains enough information to answer a real question without including too much unrelated text.

For CDS storage, each LangChain document is persisted as a vector document. For Grounding, each non-empty addDocuments() call creates one parent Grounding document containing the supplied chunks. Keep the returned parent document IDs if you need to delete that content later.

Add RAG tool to your agent

Then register a retrieval tool through buildTools:

import cds from "@sap/cds";
import { tool, context } from "langchain";
import { z } from "zod";
import { vectorStore } from "./lib/vector-store.js";

const searchKnowledgeBase = tool(
  async ({ query, limit }) => {
    const documents = await vectorStore.similaritySearch(query, limit);
    if (documents.length === 0) {
      return "No relevant passages were found in the knowledge base.";
    }

    return documents
      .map(
        (document) => context`
      Source: ${document.metadata.source ?? "Unknown source"}
      Passage: ${document.pageContent}
    `,
      )
      .join("\n\n");
  },
  {
    name: "search_knowledge_base",
    description: "Find passages in the knowledge base relevant to a question.",
    schema: z.object({
      query: z.string().min(1),
      limit: z.number().int().min(1).max(10).default(4),
    }),
  },
);

export class AgentService extends cds.ApplicationService {
  init() {
    this.on("buildTools", async (req, next) => {
      const tools = await next();
      return [...tools, searchKnowledgeBase];
    });
    return super.init();
  }
}

The CAP Agent keeps its normal runtime and adds this search tool. The tool code is the same for both configurations because it uses their common text-search interface.

Using CDS-based Vector Store

 

Using SAP AI Core Document Grounding Vector Store

Note: The adapters are not identical in every operation. Document Grounding approach uses native retrieval filters and server-side embeddings. CDS approach supports its own metadata-filter operators and maximum marginal relevance search. Avoid assuming that scores, filters, or deletion arguments are interchangeable.

Choosing an approach for your application

I would start with Document Grounding when a managed grounding service is part of the architecture, especially when the team wants the knowledge base operated separately from individual application databases - imagine you have a Microsoft Sharepoint, and you want to ingest once in a while the agent to search documents stored there without importing them into your CAP application's database.

I would consider CDS storage when the content belongs to one CAP application, the team already operates its persistence, and a direct model of documents, metadata, and embeddings fits the requirement. It is a quick way to get started for a PoC or one-off usage, but its usefulness is not limited to demonstrations. It supports similarity search, metadata filtering, custom persistence entities, configurable vector dimensions, and maximum marginal relevance retrieval.

The agent needs useful evidence at the point where it answers a question. These add-ons provide two ways to retrieve that evidence while keeping the agent integration familiar: SAP AI Core Document Grounding for managed grounding, or CDS persistence for a knowledge base operated with your CAP application.

You can explore the source code and examples, try the approach that fits your application, and share feedback or issues in the repository.

entry.title: Agentic AI Needs an Environment: Lessons from PaPM and ERP Controlling
entry.content:
For an AI to be truly agentic, it needs an environment to work in. To me, this is almost self-evident.

Connecting an LLM to data is not enough. The environment needs state, business logic, functions the agent can call, and a way to receive feedback from a human. Only then can the AI do more than answer a question. It can move toward a goal: look at what is happening, decide what to do next, run the right function, inspect the result, spot a problem, form a hypothesis, and test it.

By this definition, both a calculation model in SAP Profitability and Performance Management (PaPM) and the Controlling module in ERP can serve as environments for agentic AI.

1. The PaPM calculation model as an environment

In PaPM, the calculation is stored in a narrative form. Functions embed the methodology, and the methodology consists of a preparation phase and the factor analysis calculation itself.

So where does the agentic part come in? I don’t see our agent as a chat that looks at a final table and writes a nicely worded report. Imagine it receives a task: run the calculation and analyze the significant variances for a specific production order. The agent then works out the steps on its own. It prepares the required data, runs the right functions, executes the calculation, looks at the result, and only then starts analyzing. Along the way it can:

  • determine which preparation functions need to run,
  • execute the right sequence of functions,
  • retrieve the result,
  • walk through the final table and find significant variances,
  • identify which factor drove each variance,
  • trace back through the model and methodology to understand how the number was produced,
  • prepare a final report for the user.

Suppose the agent notices that the standard price differs sharply from the actual one. It digs into the drivers and finds that one factor is the number of hours: 170 working hours were expected, but only 10 hours were allocated to this production order.

Context matters here. We are looking at a single production order, but cost allocation happens during period-end closing. If more production orders had been closed in the period, the costs (specifically labor costs) would have been spread across them, and the result for this order would look different.

So the agent doesn’t just say, “You have 170 planned hours against 10 actual.” It explains why this affected the result and how the figure connects to the calculation methodology: the gap between expected and allocated hours changed the cost distribution and, in turn, the outcome of the factor analysis.

When the model isn’t enough

Sometimes the information inside the PaPM model is not sufficient to find the real cause. This is where I also see agentic behavior. The agent must not invent a cause and present it as fact. It should say something like:

“A possible reason is how the actual production time was recorded in ERP.” (a hypothesis)

Then it needs to figure out how to verify that hypothesis, and tell the human where to look:

“Check production order X in ERP. Review the confirmed production time and the source it came from in the calculation.”

The agent is no longer just answering a question. It is directing a person to what needs to be checked. The person goes to ERP, confirms or rejects the hypothesis, and the loop continues.

This points to an important architectural principle. ERP is our source of truth, so the LLM must never decide on its own that a hypothesis is a fact. Once a human confirms the cause, we can use that information going forward. And we don’t necessarily need to copy ERP data into PaPM or replicate anything. We can create a new view on the PaPM side that gives the agent access to the relevant ERP information. Next time, the agent can consult that source and include it in its analysis.

The full cycle looks like this:

calculation result → model analysis → missing information → hypothesis → next step → verification in ERP → human confirmation → new access to the needed information → next analysis with that context

That, for me, is where agentic AI appears. Not in the LLM’s ability to write fluent text, but in the agent’s ability to understand what to do next, what information it lacks, where to go, what to check, and how to continue once it has an answer. The agent can also do more than analyze a finished result. It can run the calculation itself by executing the sequence of methodology functions in PaPM.

2. The Controlling module in ERP

In ERP this is, in my view, even more obvious. The agent operates inside the system that is the source of truth. It knows which controlling tables exist, what they mean, how they relate, which processes exist, and which functions it can call. So it can perform concrete tasks, not just analyze:

  • create a cost center,
  • check an existing cost center,
  • validate an allocation function,
  • verify that data is configured correctly,
  • execute period-end closing steps,
  • work with reporting and the Review Booklet,
  • search for root causes of variances.

Period-end closing shows this best. The goal is simple to state: close the period. But that is not a single function call. It is a sequence of actions: check that all prerequisites are met, including settlement, then check the data, find errors or blockers, run the necessary functions, verify again, and move on.

When something goes wrong, the agent must decide what to do next. For example:

closing → error in allocation → analyze the allocation function → find a missing cost center → depending on what is being allocated, determine which master data is missing → fix it → rerun allocation → check the result → continue closing

This shows what agentic means: goal → planning → action → observe the outcome → decide what’s next → revise the plan if needed.

Our PaPM agent does exactly the same thing. The difference is only in which functions it runs. In ERP, they belong to a business process such as period closing. In PaPM, they belong to the calculation model, accessed through Joule for PaPM and then through Joule Work, a kind of universal workstation connected to the different systems in the landscape.

3. So what is the difference between PaPM and ERP?

For me, the difference is not that one scenario is agentic and the other isn’t. Both can be. The environments are simply different.

In ERP, the agent sits where the business state and the source of truth live, so it doesn’t need extra views to reach the root cause. In PaPM, the agent has the calculation model, methodology, functions, and results, but part of the information needed to explain a root cause lives in ERP. At some point the agent may conclude: “I understand the calculation, but I lack the information to explain the cause.” Then it has to go further.

Put simply:

  • ERP tells us what is happening in the business.
  • PaPM shows how the calculated result was produced.
  • The agent works out why the result looks the way it does, what is missing, and what to do next.

Why this is more than an “analytical assistant”

I wouldn’t call this agent merely an analytical assistant. Yes, it helps users with analytics, but the core idea is different.

Today, a person walks through multiple transactions, exports several Excel files, compares tables, calculates things, finds a variance, goes to another system to verify the cause, and finally assembles a report. The point of an agent is to take the human out of that routine sequence of actions.

The same goal applies to an agent handling period closing. Today a person runs the functions, checks the results, hunts for errors, and decides what to do next. The agent should do that work instead.

That is why I see no fundamental difference between these two flows:

closing → run allocation → check → run settlement → check → finish closing

run PaPM preparation phase → run calculation → review result → find variance → understand cause → request additional information → verify it → continue analysis

Behaviorally, it is the same logic: there is a goal, there is a set of available actions, and the agent chooses what to do next, observes the result, and continues.

This is also why I believe that preparing an important prerequisite for the calculation with a colleague was a real step forward. Yes, a person can walk through transactions and export a number of Excel files to build a report. But then the question is: why do we need an agent at all? The answer is that a person should no longer have to do this. The agent should own the whole process.

The idea may not have been fully understood at first, because it is somewhat indirect. I am not trying to build yet another chat that tells users a nice story about what happened. I want an assistant that performs the sequence of actions a human performs today.

The LLM is there to understand context, interpret information, form hypotheses, decide on next steps, and connect different sources. ERP and PaPM remain the systems that hold the business itself and the calculation logic.

That is why I see agentic AI as an intelligent layer on top of existing systems, not a replacement for them. That, in the end, is the whole point.

entry.title: Teched2026-XP266 -- Ship your own sandboxed AI operations agent to Kyma in two hours
entry.content:
Bring your own agent to a contained SAP Kyma sandbox with OpenRouter

Plug OpenRouter - a public LLM aggregator - into a contained sandbox with three off-the-shelf coding agents powered by free NVIDIA Nemotron models

This is a follow-up to Teched2026-XP266 | Giving an AI agent a shell — without giving away the keys to your cluster.
That post built the contained sandbox on SAP Kyma: the box is the boundary, three trust tiers, and an agent that reasons through a frontier model it never holds the key to.
Here we add a fourth tier — an external provider — and run somebody else's coding agents on a free public model, without loosening a single guarantee.

TL;DR

  • The sandbox model generalizes. "The in-cluster LLM proxy" was never special — it was just one provider. Swap in OpenRouter (a public aggregator) and the box behaves identically: one allow-listed host, nothing else.
  • Bring the model, not the key. The real OpenRouter key lives only in the gateway. Inside the box the agent carries a sentinel; the supervisor swaps it for the real key at the wire, only for a listed binary → a listed host.
  • Three off-the-shelf agents, one image, a free model. opencode, Pi, and Qwen Code — all pointed at free NVIDIA Nemotron models on OpenRouter.
  • Containment holds with a public host in the mix. The box reaches openrouter.ai and nothing else — not the internet at large, not the API server. We prove it with three curls.
  • "External" isn't "less contained." Opening one host for named binaries, with the key injected at the wire, is a different tier — not a looser one.
  • The abstraction was the product. The sandbox never cared whether the model was in-cluster or across the planet; "provider" is the seam, and it holds.
  • A free model is a confident junior. Great for a first draft, wrong about anything niche — so make the cluster the reviewer, not the reader.

Contents

  • ⚖️ The itch
  • 🧭 The fourth tier
  • 👀 See it first
  • 🧩 How it works — profile → provider → sandbox
  • 🔍 The deep dive
    • 3a. The profile is the policy
    • 3b. The provider holds the key
    • 3c. The sandbox gets a sentinel
    • 3d. Picking a free model
  • ️🛡️ Still contained — with a public host in the mix
  • 🎯 Why it's worth it
  • 🧰 Reusable patterns
  • 📎 Appendix
  • 📚 References & BOM
  • 📖 Lexicon
  • 🎓 See it live — SAP TechEd 2026 (XP266)

⚖️ The itch — one more model, one more key

👉The first post left the agent talking to SAP AI Core, in-cluster, through an in-cluster LLM proxy — no key in the box, no route to the internet.

👉However, sooner or later someone will need a feature the in-cluster proxy doesn't bridge yet, for instance:

  • a public aggregator,
  • a shiny free model to prototype with,
  • an off-the-shelf coding agent that only knows how to talk to OpenRouter.

👉So the question remains:

How do you let an agent use an external model — reached over the public internet — without putting the key in the box or opening a route it can abuse?

👉The answer turns out to be not a new mechanism at all.

🧭 The fourth tier — an external provider

The first post had three tiers — the same sandbox image, with each tier granting a bit more access - the more you trust the workload. 

TierReachesClusterLLM Key in sandbox
1. Containedthe in-cluster LLM onlynonenone (sentinel)
2. Scoped-ops+ API server (read-only)read-only kubectlnone (sentinel)
3. Web terminalfull pod networkRBAC-scoped kubectlnone (sentinel)

This external provider adds a fourth tier — same pattern adding one more row:

TierReachesClusterLLM Key in sandbox
4. External agentone public host (openrouter.ai)nonenone (sentinel)

👉And it is not a weaker tier — it's a different one.

  • The box still can't reach the API server or the rest of the internet. 
  • And the only thing that changed is which single endpoint the supervisor opens, and that the credential behind it is a real OpenRouter key — held, as always, by the gateway and never by the box.

👀 See it first — from the web terminal

  • Kyma web terminal embeds the openshell CLI
  • the terminal runs inside the cluster, thus, you reach the gateway's Service directly (no HTTPS host, no port-forward).
  • The openshell gateway is OIDC-gated; it validates your Keycloak token itself.
  • The terminal has no browser, so you log in with the device-code flow:

 

export XP266_CLUSTER=xp266-NNN          # your runtime number
export XP266_DOMAIN=<workshop-domain>   # handed out at the session

OPENSHELL_NO_BROWSER=1 openshell gateway add http://openshell.openshell.svc.cluster.local:8080 \
  --oidc-issuer https://keycloak.$XP266_CLUSTER.$XP266_DOMAIN/realms/ateam-isveng \
  --oidc-client-id openshell-oidc
#   To authenticate, visit:
#     https://keycloak.<cluster>.<domain>/realms/ateam-isveng/device?user_code=XXXX-XXXX
#   ✓ Authenticated via device code      ← approve on your laptop, you need the `openshell-admin` role

👉pick a current free model and create the sandbox:

 

export FREE_MODEL=nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free   # a current :free NVIDIA model

openshell sandbox create --name agents \
  --from localhost:32137/openrouter-agents:latest \
  --provider openrouter \
  --env OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 \
  --env OPENAI_MODEL=$FREE_MODEL \
  --detach -- sleep infinity &
openshell sandbox list        # wait for PHASE=Ready
👉--provider openrouter is the whole trick: it opens egress to openrouter.ai (+ models.dev) for the agent binaries only, and injects the key sentinel.

👉Run any of the three agents — same box, same model:

# opencode (open-source Bun agent):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- opencode run -m openrouter/$FREE_MODEL "Reply with one word: PONG"
#   PONG

# Pi (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- pi -p --model openrouter/$FREE_MODEL "List 3 facts about Kyma."

# Qwen Code (OpenAI-compatible — takes no -m; reads $OPENAI_MODEL):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- qwen -p "List 3 facts about Kyma."
 

👉An off-the-shelf coding agent just reasoned through a frontier-grade free model.

Now the punchline: try to break out

openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- sh -c '
  curl -sS -m8 -o /dev/null -w "openrouter.ai: %{http_code}\n" https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models
  curl -sS -m8 https://example.com            >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "example.com: REACHED" || echo "example.com: blocked"
  curl -sS -m8 https://kubernetes.default.svc >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "apiserver: REACHED"   || echo "apiserver: blocked"
  echo "key in box: $OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
 
openrouter.ai: 200
example.com: blocked                     ← the rest of the internet: no route
apiserver: blocked                       ← the cluster API: no route
key in box: openshell:resolve:env:…      ← a sentinel, NOT the real key

👉One host reachable.

  • ✅Everything else refused.
  • ✅The key never in the box.
  • ✅That's the fourth tier in three curl lines.

🧩 How it works — profile → provider → sandbox

Three concepts, one key that never leaves the gateway:

  • Profile — a reusable spec, no secret in it: which credential env var, which auth style, which endpoints egress may reach, and which binaries are allowed to use the credential.
  • Provider — a profile bound to a real key. The key (sk-or-…) is stored only in the gateway.
  • Sandbox — --provider openrouter attaches it: the box receives a sentinel (not the key) + scoped egress; the supervisor swaps the sentinel for the real key at the wire, only for a listed binary reaching a listed endpoint.
 

 

Same picture, in ASCII, for renderers that don't do Mermaid:

   ┌───────────────── OpenShell gateway (holds the real key) ───────────────── ┐
   │ profile "openrouter"   credential: OPENROUTER_API_KEY (bearer)            │
   │                        endpoints : openrouter.ai, models.dev  ← only hosts│
   │                        binaries  : node, opencode, qwen, pi   ← only these│
   │ provider "openrouter" = profile + REAL KEY           ← key lives ONLY here│
   └───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                 sandbox create --provider openrouter
                                        ▼
   ┌──────────────────── your sandbox (the box) ────────────────────┐
   │ OPENROUTER_API_KEY = openshell:resolve:…   ← a SENTINEL        │
   │ agent  ──▶  Authorization: Bearer <sentinel>                   │
   └───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                        ▼ (allowed binary + allowed host)
            supervisor swaps  <sentinel> → sk-or-…  AT THE WIRE
                                        ▼
                                  openrouter.ai   (sees the real key; the box never did)
 
In a nutshell:
  • 👉The gateway is the keeper of secrets
  • 👉the profile is the policy
  • 👉the sentinel is what the agent gets instead of a key.

🔍 The deep dive

3a. The profile is the policy (endpoints × binaries)

  • A profile answers two questions and nothing else: which hosts may this credential reach, and which binaries may send that traffic.
  • For OpenRouter that's openrouter.ai (the inference API) plus models.dev (opencode's model-registry metadata, dialed on startup), and the agent binaries (node, opencode, qwen, pi).
  • Everything outside that cross product is denied by default — a block-list would be a guessing game; an allow-list is a decision you can read.

3b. The provider holds the key — once, in one place

  • The provider is the profile plus a real key.
  • On OpenShell 0.1.1 the key is injected into the box as a resolve-sentinel (openshell:resolve:env:…); the supervisor resolves it to the real sk-or-… only at egress, and only for an allowed binary → an allowed host.
  • The two env vars the agents read — OPENROUTER_API_KEY (Pi, opencode) and OPENAI_API_KEY (the OpenAI-compatible Qwen Code) — both carry the sentinel.
  • Compromise the agent and all you've got is the string openshell:resolve:env:….

3c. The sandbox gets a sentinel, never the secret

  • This is the same credential-injection trick from the first post, now across a public hop instead of an in-cluster one.
  • The box's view of the world: an env var that looks like a key but isn't, and exactly one host it's allowed to send it to.
  • The agent can't tell the difference — it sets Authorization: Bearer <sentinel> and the reply comes back — but an attacker who owns the agent gets a placeholder and a single, logged, allow-listed destination.

3d. Picking a free model

OpenRouter's :free tier includes NVIDIA's Nemotron family — frontier-grade, no quota spent.

  • The agents call tools, so the model must be a chat/completion model with tool-calling. Embedding/rerank models (ids with -embed- / -rerank-) are RAG parts, not chat — the agent will error.
  • Two known-good picks: nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free (large, higher quality) and nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free (smaller, faster).

🛡️ Still contained — with a public host in the mix

  • 👉 The instinct is that "the box can now reach the internet" must mean "the box is less safe."
  • 👉 It doesn't — because the internet was never opened.

Here's what each familiar threat runs into:

ThreatWhat usually enables itWhat this tier does instead
Data exfiltrationthe agent has the internetone host resolves (openrouter.ai); example.com and everything else → no route
Reaching the clusterpod → API server pathno route to kubernetes.default.svc — this tier grants no cluster access at all
Credential theftthe agent holds the keythe key is never in the box — a sentinel in, the real sk-or-… injected at the last hop
A rogue binary phoning homeany process can egressegress is binary-scoped — only node/opencode/qwen/pi may send; anything else is denied
Silent abuseno audit trailevery denied request is logged at the supervisor

 

 

🎯 Why it's worth it

You can say yes to a much wider set of "can the agent use this model?" questions, because "use" now happens somewhere it can't hurt you — even when the model lives on the public internet behind a paid key:

  • ✅ off-the-shelf coding agents (opencode, Pi, Qwen Code) you didn't write and don't fully trust, run safely
  • ✅ free models for prototyping and workshops — no quota, no standing credential in the box
  • ✅ the same contained guarantees as the in-cluster tier: one host, no cluster, key in the gateway
  • ✅ a clean generalization — "provider" means any governed endpoint, in-cluster or external, by the same rules

All on the stock OpenShell chart and agent-sandbox controller, on a normal managed Kyma cluster.

🧰 Reusable patterns

Strip out OpenRouter and several of these stand on their own — a toolkit for governing any external dependency a semi-trusted workload needs.

  • Model the credential as a profile, not an env var. Separate the spec (which hosts, which binaries, which auth) from the secret. The spec is reviewable in Git; the secret lives in exactly one guarded place. ✅ You can audit "what can reach the internet" without ever seeing a key.
  •  Scope egress by binary, not just by host. "node and opencode may reach openrouter.ai" is a far tighter statement than "the pod may reach openrouter.ai." A rogue process in the box still can't send. ✅ Lateral egress inside the box is closed, not just lateral network.
  • Inject credentials at the wire — even across a public hop. The workload carries a sentinel; the proxy swaps in the real value on the last hop out. Works identically whether the destination is in-cluster or on the internet. ✅ Compromise the workload and the attacker gets the word "placeholder".
  • One proxy, two shapes. OpenAI-compatible gateways (SAP AI Core, OpenRouter) look the same to a proxy — so one in-cluster exit can front both, spend-tracked, keys never leaving it. ✅ Add a provider without adding an egress path.
  • Free tiers make experimentation cheap — pin against their churn. A :free model is perfect for a workshop or a spike; its instability is the price. Keep a fallback and list-before-you-run. ✅ Zero-cost iteration, with a documented escape hatch when a model goes paid.
  • Let the platform adjudicate generated code. For anything an LLM writes against a niche API, make the API server the gate: --dry-run=server before trust. The draft→reject→fix loop is the workflow. ✅ The model's confidence stops mattering; the cluster's acceptance is the only verdict.

👉The recipe, in one line:

credential-as-profile → binary-scoped egress → sentinel-at-the-wire → one proxy, two shapes → free tier with a fallback → the cluster adjudicates generated code.

📎 Appendix

 

A. The provider profile (what --provider openrouter binds to)

Wired once per gateway (the real key is handed to the gateway here and never leaves it):

  • The profile lists the endpoints egress may reach (openrouter.ai, models.dev) and the binaries allowed to use the credential; the provider is that profile plus the real sk-or-….
  • Inside the box the agents see only the sentinel in OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY;
  • The supervisor resolves it at egress for an allowed binary → an allowed host.

The profile itself (imported into the gateway) — the whole policy is the endpoint × binary cross-product:

 

id: openrouter
display_name: OpenRouter
inference_capable: true
credentials:
  - name: api_key
    env_vars: [OPENROUTER_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY]   # agents read either; injected as a resolve-sentinel, swapped at egress
    auth_style: bearer
    header_name: authorization
endpoints:
  - { host: openrouter.ai, port: 443, protocol: rest, access: read-write }   # the inference API (/api/v1/…)
  - { host: models.dev,    port: 443, protocol: rest, access: read-only }    # opencode's model registry (dialed on startup)
binaries:
  - /usr/local/bin/node                                        # Pi + Qwen Code — the connecting process is node
  - /usr/local/bin/opencode                                    # opencode launcher symlink
  - /usr/local/lib/node_modules/opencode-ai/bin/opencode.exe   # opencode's RESOLVED Bun ELF (the symlink alone fails)

Why both OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY?

👉 Because the three agents expect the key under different env-var names, and listing both makes the gateway inject the sentinel under each — so whichever name an agent reads, it finds it:

  • OPENROUTER_API_KEY → Pi and opencode (OpenRouter-native).
  • OPENAI_API_KEY → Qwen Code, which is an OpenAI-compatible client and reads the OpenAI name.

Binding the real key turns the profile into a provider: 

The key is read from an in-cluster Secret and handed to the gateway once — it is stored only there, and every sandbox created --provider openrouter receives the sentinel, never the key.

(No tls: on the endpoints — the supervisor terminates TLS transparently and injects a CA bundle: CURL_CA_BUNDLE / NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS.)

 

B. The tools image — built in-cluster by kaniko

openrouter-agents:latest is built inside the cluster by kaniko (no CI, no registry credentials), from a Dockerfile that lives inline in a ConfigMap.

The three agents are the whole payload:

FROM node:24-bookworm-slim
# bash + CA certs for TLS to openrouter.ai; fd + ripgrep pre-installed so the agents' search tools work WITHOUT
# sandbox-blocked downloads; git for repo awareness; curl.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      bash ca-certificates fd-find git ripgrep curl \
 && ln -s /usr/bin/fdfind /usr/local/bin/fd && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# Pi + Qwen Code — pure-JS, installed with --ignore-scripts (supply-chain hygiene, no postinstall):
RUN npm install -g --ignore-scripts "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@latest"
RUN npm install -g --ignore-scripts "@qwen-code/qwen-code@latest"
# opencode — postinstall ALLOWED so it fetches the correct glibc platform binary for this base → /usr/local/bin/opencode:
RUN npm install -g --allow-scripts=opencode-ai "opencode-ai@latest"
# OpenShell 0.1.x runs the sandbox as uid 10001: add a passwd entry so $USER/$HOME resolve + a writable home:
RUN echo 'agent:x:10001:0:agent sandbox:/home/agent:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd \
 && mkdir -p /home/agent /tmp/pi-agent && chmod -R 0777 /home/agent /tmp/pi-agent
WORKDIR /home/agent
ENV PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR=/tmp/pi-agent
 

C. OpenRouter vs SAP AI Core — the same shape

Why does an external provider slot in so cleanly?

  • Because OpenRouter and SAP AI Core are the same shape to a proxy: an OpenAI-compatible gateway behind one credential.
  • OpenRouter is a public aggregator (one endpoint, many upstreams — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Qwen, NVIDIA…)
  • SAP AI Core is SAP's managed inference gateway, reached in-cluster through a proxy.

So OpenRouter is just another provider — no new integration, the same sentinel-at-the-wire mechanism.

 SAP AI Core (via in-cluster LLM proxy)OpenRouter (via direct path)
Pathagent → in-cluster proxy → SAP AI Coreagent → OpenRouter (one allow-listed external host)
Key in boxnone — a sentinel (real key in the gateway)none — a sentinel (real key in the gateway)
Internetnoneone host: openrouter.ai

In summary:

  • 👉The key story is identical — in both, the real credential lives only in the gateway and the box carries a sentinel.
  • 👉The only things that differ are the egress path (an in-cluster service vs one public host) and whether any internet is opened at all.
  • ⚠️The one thing that does not work: OpenRouter cannot call SAP AI Core. OpenRouter only routes to its own public upstreams — it can't reach an in-cluster proxy.
